title: Evaluating Deep Learning Models
html:
Measure on data the model never trained on, in eval mode, with the metric that matches the real goal. Loss tells you how training is going; task metrics tell you whether the model is useful.

Three splits

SplitUsed forTouched
TrainingComputing gradientsEvery step
ValidationEarly stopping, hyper-parameters, model selectionEvery epoch
TestFinal, unbiased estimateOnce, at the end
Watch out

Tuning on the test set turns it into a second validation set — the final number becomes optimistic. Also watch for leakage: near-duplicate images, the same patient/user in two splits, or time series split randomly instead of by time.

From logits to metrics

TaskMetrics
ClassificationAccuracy, precision/recall/F1 (per class, macro/weighted), ROC-AUC, top-k accuracy, confusion matrix
RegressionMAE, RMSE, R²
Detection / segmentationmAP (mean average precision), IoU, Dice
Language modelsPerplexity = exp(mean cross-entropy), plus task benchmarks
GenerationFID (images), BLEU/ROUGE (text), human or LLM-judge evaluation

Beyond one number

  • Calibration — does 90% confidence mean right 90% of the time? Deep nets are often over-confident; temperature scaling on the validation set fixes much of it.
  • Slices — accuracy per class, per demographic, per data source; averages hide failures.
  • Error analysis — look at the worst mistakes (see Error Analysis in the Machine Learning notes).
  • Variance — rerun with a few seeds; differences smaller than seed-to-seed noise aren't real.
  • Cost — latency, memory and throughput at inference matter as much as accuracy in production.
Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?

If 99% of transactions are legitimate, predicting “legit” for everything scores 99% while catching zero fraud. Use per-class precision/recall, F1, PR-AUC and a confusion matrix instead.

What is perplexity?

The exponential of the average per-token cross-entropy of a language model. It's the effective number of equally likely choices the model is torn between at each step — lower is better.
